concept.name: Term premium
concept.definition: The extra yield investors demand for holding a longer-term bond instead of rolling over a series of short-term instruments — compensation for the risk that future rates and inflation differ from expectations. It is the difference between a long-term yield and the expected average of future short rates, and it is not directly observable.
concept.intuition: Locking your money up for ten years is riskier than renewing a one-year loan ten times; the term premium is the extra pay for bearing that risk.
concept.mechanics: Estimated with term-structure models: a model (e.g. the Fed's Kim–Wright three-factor arbitrage-free model, published on FRED as THREEFYTP10) decomposes observed yields into expected short-rate paths plus a residual term premium. Estimates are model-dependent and can be negative.
concept.formula: y(T) ≈ (1/T) × Σ E[short rate_t] + TP(T), where y(T) is the T-year yield and TP(T) the term premium.
concept.failure_modes: Term premium estimates vary substantially across models and can flip sign with specification changes; using any single estimate as ground truth for 'rich/cheap' bonds is fragile.
concept.misconceptions: The term premium is not a measured quantity like a yield — it is a model-implied residual, and a rising long yield does not tell you whether expectations or the premium moved without a model.
concept.example: If the 10-year Treasury yields 4.5% while the expected average short rate over the decade is 4.0%, the model-implied 10-year term premium is about 0.5%.

citations.source: FRED, Term Premium on a 10 Year Zero Coupon Bond [THREEFYTP10] (source: Board of Governors, Kim and Wright 2005)
